get.description:
**DEF-650 — THE CHECK AT PREMISES CREATION, as an endpoint.**

PO 2026-08-27: *"it can be existing master account also so at the time of
premises creation we should check - how you will handle this"*. This is how:
the wizard asks before it creates, and gets one of three answers.

``?name=Ridge Property LLC`` →
  ``{"match": "exact", "owner": {...}, "candidates": []}``  reuse this party
  ``{"match": "near",  "owner": null,  "candidates": [...]}``  the clerk picks
  ``{"match": "none",  "owner": null,  "candidates": []}``  nobody by that name

GET and read-only: it takes no decision, it reports one. The clerk takes the
decision, which is PO decision 3 (*"offer the match, clerk decides"*) made
structural rather than promised in a comment.

**PRM-04 - BR-MET-151's review surface, and it IS the flagged migration.**

`metering 0040` writes no owner row, because the PO's caveat says so in as
many words: *"They are real data on a live tenant. A flagged migration that
offers each name for matching is the shape; silently guessing which string
is which party is not."* This endpoint is the offer -- every free-text owner
name that still points at no typed party, grouped BY NAME so twelve
addresses sharing one landlord are one decision rather than twelve.

It offers CANDIDATES and never a CATEGORY. `suggested_owner_ids` holds only
exact case-insensitive name matches; a fuzzy suggestion is a guess wearing a
suggestion's clothes, and a clerk working down a list will accept it.

post.description:
**DEF-650 — declare the ACCOUNT this owner is billed through.**

`{"account_id": "<uuid>"}` links; `{"account_id": null}` clears. It never
creates an account: `accounts` is customers' table (B1/B2 §2), and the PO's
own case is an account that ALREADY EXISTS.
Staged preview: every row validated, NOTHING written (BR-MET-004).

Commit with skip-errors ON by default; the "N created · N failed"
summary is ALWAYS in the body (BR-MET-038).

get.description:
CR-089 wave B (`B7`/`PUJ-08`) — the premise number the review shows.

The premises twin of `unit_number_preview` above and the same rule
(`BR-MET-1165`): it allocates nothing, advances nothing and locks nothing.
Two clerks reviewing at the same moment are both shown `P-00080`; the second
to press gets `P-00081`. The reasoning, and why it does not read
`number_series.next_number` directly, is in `services.preview_premise_number`.

`GET /premises/owner-search?q=&page=&per=` — `CR-177-BRC10` task 1b.

The utility's MASTER accounts by name or account number, PAGED (NFR-3, no
cap): account number, name, account type, person or company, managed by,
status. Customers answers the account half through metering's read-only
seam; **Managed by is metering's own fact** — the `owner_manager` recorded
on the premises this account already owns — read once for the page.

`GET /premises/picker?q=&page=&per=` — **the register's own search, for
any screen that PICKS an address rather than typing one.**

PO ruling 2026-09-15: *"if we have unit or street address then we should
take it from premises/Unit - it means its a search and if not foudn them
alow user to add them"*. Capture step 3 is its first caller; move-in,
transfer and the owner's-account path want the same search.

⚠ **THE QUERYSET IS HANDED TO THE PAGINATOR UNEVALUATED, AND THAT IS THE
POINT.** `_page` above does `list(rows)` first, which pulls every premises
the tenant has into memory before slicing — invisible at 79 properties and
the shape of `NFR-3`'s existing breaches at the top of T5 (40,000). DRF
slices a QuerySet with `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` and counts it with one `COUNT(*)`,
so this read costs the page and not the register.

Nothing about meters, services or accounts is in the answer — the same
ruling's second clause puts those on the move-in request.

`GET /premises/same-address?address_line=&city=&state=&postal_code=` —
`CR-177-BRC10` task 1 · `BR-MET-1190`.

`{"same": {premise_no, address, units, status, id} | null}`. The screen asks
it as the clerk completes the address; `create_premises` asks the SAME
function again at the write, so the two cannot disagree. A pure read, scoped
to the tenant (hard rule 1). `id` is for the *Open it* link only (B14 rule
31); the premise NUMBER and the address are what a clerk reads.

BR-MET-034: the premises-types Reference-data list. Served here because
tenancy's LOOKUP_LISTS registry has no 'premises_types' key to register
against (reported).

`GET /premises/{id}/build` — the build at this address, or `null`.

Every figure is metering's own derivation, called by name through the seam;
nothing is computed here and nothing is defaulted. `{"build": null}` when
there is no build, and the screen says so in a sentence rather than drawing
an empty Build tab (law 2).

CR-089 wave E (`E3`/`PUJ-23`) — what a building lends to the units added
to it: its identity, what is on it today, the services it offers and the
routes its units join. A pure read; see `selectors.premises_lends_dict`.

post.description:
One address, one name, one person's decision (BR-MET-151).

`{"owner_id": ...}` links an existing party; anything else CREATES one, and
the caller always supplies the category. The premises' `owner_manager` is
left exactly as it was -- it is the provenance of the match and what
`open_account` reads for the default payer (`OQ-500`).

`{status, effective_date, reason}` — all three required, both directions.

The refusal, the date rules and the audit row are the SERVICE's; this view
decides nothing.

get.description:
What the status dialog draws BEFORE it asks: the live counts, whether the
commit is held, and which count is holding it.

⚠ **A READ, DELIBERATELY SEPARATE FROM THE WRITE.** The counts have to be
taken at the moment the dialog opens (BR-MET-1164 refuses on LIVE
dependencies), and folding them into the premises detail payload would make
every property page pay for four extra reads it does not draw.

**CR-038 W6 — BR-MET-125's report: master vs Σ sub-meters, per period.**

PO verbatim, 2026-08-26: *"Open 9 - (a) store + report — keeps the door
open"*. The worked figure this reports: master **12,400 kWh** − Σ subs
**11,940** = **460 kWh (3.71%)** against a **3%** tolerance.

`?period=YYYY-MM` (or `YYYY-MM-DD`) narrows to one reading month; without it
every stored period answers, newest first, with `periods` listing the months
that actually have a row.

**It serves STORED rows and recomputes nothing** — see the selector for why
that is the point rather than a shortcut.

House URL grammar (resource, then subpath). The A11 row for this route is
OWED — see the exceptions trailer.

`CR-176-BRC10` rule (1) — the first number from which a run of
`count` units (× `floors`, labelled by `label_pattern`) is wholly free at
this building. The Add units screen defaults *Start numbering at* to it and
prints *Next free: N*. A pure read: nothing is reserved, so two clerks may
both be told 6 and the second press is refused naming the labels — the
same posture `BR-MET-1165` takes for unit numbers.

`GET /premises/{id}/work-orders` — every job at this address.

Every anchor, every state, newest first. The premises is the host that
ALWAYS exists (execution plan judgment 1), and **that judgment stands on the
column being OPTIONAL rather than on its writer being missing.**
`connections.owner_account_id` is nullable; a build may carry no owner
account because nobody named an owner, or because `BR-MET-116` refuses one on
a build with no common area by design. An account-only host would render an
empty screen for any of those builds.

⚠ **THIS PARAGRAPH SAID `create_owner_account()` RAISES
`NotImplementedError("OQ-373")` UNTIL 2026-09-12 (`DEF-MET-5081`).** It does
not, and has not since `OQ-373` closed on 2026-08-25 → `BR-MET-116`. The
figure was right and the reason was wrong: measured with `app.tenant_id`
set, **8 `brazosbend` connections, 0 with an owner account** — because the
fixture seeds connection rows directly rather than committing them through
`commit_connection` step 4.

A cross-tenant id yields an empty page rather than a 404 here, and that is
the same sentence as *"nothing has happened at this address"*: the seam
filters by the tenant in context with RLS `FORCE` underneath, so Lone Star
Ridge cannot learn that one of Brazos Bend's premises exists (hard rule 1).

post.description:
`POST /protections/{id}/lift` — end a hold early, with a reason.

The reason is required by the service and is not defaulted here: lifting the
thing that stands between a household and a cut is a decision somebody has
to be able to reconstruct in a year (hard rule 7).

Keyed by PROTECTION id and not by account, because an account can carry more
than one and lifting "the protection on this account" would be ambiguous on
exactly the accounts where it matters most.

get.description:
`DEF-RAT-9797` (PO ruling 2026-10-06: a rate schedule names exactly one
base charge code) — the live schedules that name none while their service
has one. Since 2026-10-06 (`DEF-RAT-9832`, PO ruling) they bill a `$0.00`
base with a warning until a System Admin chooses — no code is taken from
the pool; this is what the Rate schedules notice counts and names.

Unpaginated on its own facts: bounded by the tenant's own live schedules
(tens), and it is a to-do list whose length IS the message.

**Based on** — which services this schedule may take a percentage OF.
`CR-130-BRC07` §3 · PO ruling 2026-09-22.

`?service=<code>&basis=usage|charge`. The list is DERIVED from what the
tenant has switched on and from what the chosen basis can actually supply
(`selectors.percent_basis_options`); **no service code appears in any
condition**, which is the ruling — *"dont hard code anything - use logic to
derive it so that it is flexible and handle any scenario."*

⚠ **IT EXISTS SO THE DERIVATION IS NOT WRITTEN TWICE.** The wizard already
receives every enabled service with its `billing_basis` on the Settings
payload and could filter client-side — and that is precisely the shape
CLAUDE.md's hard-won law 2 names: the front end types the service list out
by hand in two places, so an eleventh service *"does NOT appear on screen on
its own and it fails SILENTLY"*. One answer, served, is one place to fix.

A READ, gated as one (`AnyTenantRole`), and unpaginated by SHAPE rather
than by size: it returns the tenant's enabled services, which `BR-RAT-024`
caps at the platform catalogue's eleven. `NFR-3` is about lists that grow
with the utility; this one cannot.

post.description:
DEF-RAT-6447 — throw away the parked draft, keep the live rate.

POST rather than DELETE because the schedule is not what is being deleted:
the draft is one row inside it and the answer is the schedule as it now
stands, which is what the wizard reloads from.

DEF-370 · CR-013 part 1's *"Duplicate (the normal way to start a
filing)"*. 201 with a Location on the NEW schedule, because that is what was
created — the source is read and never written.

get.description:
CR-013 part 1 step 4's MANDATORY impact analysis (DEF-434).

Part 1, verbatim: *"effective/end dates plus mandatory impact analysis:
accounts affected by plan, average and worst-case bill change per class,
annualised revenue change, accounts over threshold"*, glossed as *"MANDATORY
and is four figures, not a warning banner"*. Until this route existed
`GET /rate-schedules/{id}` served `used_by_plans` and `applied_to_accounts`
and nothing else, so three of the four figures were stated absences on the
screen and BR-RAT-091 clause 2's `10%` gate read a number nobody computed.

A READ, and gated as one (`AnyTenantRole`, like every other rating read):
it prices, it does not write, and a clerk who may look at a rate schedule
may look at what changing it would do. The ENFORCEMENT lives on the write —
`services.create_rate_schedule_version` — so nothing depends on a client
having asked this question first.

`effective_from` (ISO date) and `version_id` are both optional. The default
is the schedule's saved draft, or its latest version, compared against
whatever it replaces.

`CR-157-BRC10` wave B — the Plans tab: Plan · Code · Customer class ·
Status · Units, with *Class differs*. PAGED IN SQL (`NFR-3`): the paginator
is handed a queryset, so `count` is a `COUNT(*)` and only the page is
enriched. It replaces the tab's client-side scan of the first 200 plans.
No filters, no sort — the drawing draws one table with no toolbar.

`CR-157-BRC10` wave B — the Rates tab's *Base charges* table and the
*Sizes priced* tile, for the schedule as it stands today
(`schedule_reads.schedule_rates`). A READ, gated as one.

Unpaginated by SHAPE: one row per connection size THIS schedule prices,
which is bounded by the tenant's size catalogue for one service (water has
five, trash seven) and does not grow with accounts — `NFR-3` is about lists
that grow with the utility. The Units column is one grouped count, however
many units are on the schedule.

post.description:
`BR-RAT-1016` verb 2 — correct a LIVE version over the SAME window.

⚠ **IT IS A POST TO A COLLECTION AND NOT A PATCH, AND THE SHAPE IS THE
RULE.** A correction MINTS a row; the corrected version is never rewritten.
The same spelling `POST /taxes/{id}/corrections` and
`POST /discounts/{id}/versions/{vid}/corrections` already use — the fifth
and last of `BR-RAT-1016`'s priced objects, answering the question the way
the other four answer it. Two objects answering one question two ways is
the whole finding the PO was shown.

Deliberately NOT a flag on `/versions`: one endpoint with a boolean would
let a caller turn a rate change into a correction by flipping a field.
S28 steps 1–2 — stage a batch. Nothing posts (BR-MET-012).

S28 — the supervisor CO-SIGN (OQ-042 closure, CR-038 W7 task 5).

⛔ The route exists because `cosigned_by` has been SERVED on every batch
since migration 0003 and **nothing has ever written it** — hard-won law 2,
and the reason S28's docstring says it draws no co-sign control: *"drawing
the checkbox would offer a control that changes nothing"*. Now it changes
something.

Role is enforced in the SERVICE (`@require_role(SYSTEM_ADMIN, EXECUTIVE)`)
and not by a route-level class, exactly as every other rule-bearing door in
this module does it: `AnyTenantRole` lets the request reach the rule, and
the rule answers with the role refusal a clerk can read.

⚠ It does NOT block the post. OQ-042's *"blocks when enabled"* half needs a
tenant toggle whose home is the S64 settings document another lane owns —
DEF-815, filed rather than commented.

S28 step 4 — BR-MET-051's reset across the batch's demand rows.

A technician who resets a fleet of demand registers on one visit says so
once, about the visit. The answer names every row it wrote and every row it
skipped, so the clerk who clicked can check it (CLAUDE.md rule 7).

S28 step 5 — the commit. **PARTIAL SINCE BR-MET-940 (CR-054 task 14).**

⚠ **THIS DOCSTRING SAID "the atomic commit" AND THAT IS NOW HALF TRUE, SO
IT SAYS WHICH HALF.** The TRANSACTION is still atomic — one outer
`transaction.atomic()`, so a killed process leaves nothing. What is no
longer all-or-nothing is the FILE: a row the batch cannot file is held with
a reason and the rest of the readings post, under the PO's *"all or nothing
will not work - we accept what is correct and rejct what i not correct"*.
A 1,180-row file with 2 unknown meters answers `posted_reads: 1178`,
`held_reads: 2` and a link to the file those 2 come back as.

⚠ **A SECOND POST OF THE SAME BATCH IS STILL REFUSED** (hard rule 6,
BR-MET-018) — the batch reaches `posted` whether it filed every row or
1,178 of them, and the held rows return as a corrected FILE, which is a new
batch. Nothing here can double-file a reading.

⚠ **202 ABOVE THE POST BAR (`DEF-MET-8106`, BR-MET-055).** This read
*"Synchronous today; the BR-MET-055 async wrapper is REPORTED as
outstanding"*, and 480 readings then took ~60 s inside a request the web
worker is killed at. A batch of more than `services.READ_POST_ASYNC_ROW_BAR`
staged rows now answers **202** with `job_id` + `status_url` (poll
`GET /jobs/{id}` for `progress`) and `receipt_url`, where the receipt is
collected once the job has succeeded. At or below the bar: 200 and the
receipt, exactly as before.

get.description:
`GET /read-batches/{id}/post-receipt` — what the post did (`DEF-MET-8106`).

The receipt a background post cannot hand back on the request that started
it. The batch's own fields are read fresh and the post's figures come from
`read_import_batches.post_receipt`, written in the post's own transaction —
the same dict the synchronous post answers with. 404 until the batch has
posted: a receipt for a post that has not happened is not a receipt.

`GET /read-batches/{id}/results.csv?kind=failures|successes` — **the
rejects file, and its mirror (CR-054 task 16, BR-MET-941).**

PO, carried into CR-054: *"we accept what is correct and rejct what i not
correct - then create csv file at loading stage itself so that suer can see
all cases thata re rejcted"*.

⚠ **ONE PATH AND A `kind` PARAMETER, AND THE WORDS ARE `import_results_csv`'s
OWN.** They are two representations of one resource — the batch's result —
and two endpoints would be two places for the refusals and the streaming to
drift apart (that route's own argument, and `import_sample`'s precedent
before it). The vocabulary is deliberately the account importer's rather
than words invented for reads, so a clerk who has run one migration has
already learned the other.

⚠ **`failures` IS AVAILABLE FROM `validated` ONWARD — the PO's *"at loading
stage itself"*, and `DEF-2487`'s ruling on the same file one importer over:
the one moment a person most needs the list of what failed is the moment a
commit has just fallen over, and hanging the download off the receipt screen
is what made it unreachable there. `successes` needs a post, because before
the commit nothing has landed and a header with no rows under it reads as an
ANSWER (`DEF-320`).

⚠ **IT STREAMS**, over a generator that reads the batch's rows in chunks:
`read_import.CSV_ROW_CAP` is 50,000, and a 50,000-row CSV built in memory is
`DEF-766`'s payload in a download.

⚠ **`CsvRenderer` FIRST, FOR `DEF-553`'S REASON** — `@api_view`'s default
renderers satisfy only JSON, so DRF's content negotiation refuses a
browser's `Accept` with 400 *before the view runs*. This view returns an
`HttpResponse` subclass and never calls `render`.

A READ: it writes nothing, not even an audit row. Downloading the result of
a batch is not an event (`import_results_csv` takes the same posture).

delete.description:
BR-MET-054's delete scope, and the ONLY delete verb in this module's
reads surface: a staged/rejected row of an un-posted batch. There is no
endpoint that deletes a committed read, by design (US-MET-016 TC-5/TC-6).

patch.description: S28 step 4 — one row's disposition + reason (BR-MET-015).
S28 step 4 — BR-MET-051's reset, noted on ONE demand row.

post.description: S28 step 3 — run the EP-MET-04 engine over every staged row.

get.description:
S25 — server-paginated, 2-year hot window by default (BR-MET-055).
`archive=true` is the explicit opt-in; no unbounded path exists.

`f.status=pending` (CR-038 W1 — US-MET-012 §1, verbatim: *"Pending =
plan-required record (meter × channel, BR-MET-049) with no committed read
this cycle — derived, not stored"*) serves the DERIVED pending entries —
expected registers of the open cycle windows with no committed head —
rather than filtering stored rows, because no stored row exists to filter:
a `status="pending"` queryset filter would return an empty list that reads
as "nothing pending". Each entry carries `id: null` and `derived:
"pending"` so no client mistakes it for an addressable read. Bounded by
the cycles' own membership (BR-MET-055's posture) and paged like the rest.

`GET reads/answer-questions?q=&key=&page=&per=` — the Reads list's
Answer filter vocabulary: questions of PUBLISHED formats, server-paged
(NFR-3). Any office role, because the Reads list is (a clerk filters it;
Settings → Reads is not theirs).

post.description:
`POST /reads/bulk-estimate` — estimate a SET of missing records.

Every target goes through `estimate_missing_read`, so BR-MET-026's
arithmetic, BR-MET-027's two-consecutive limit and BR-MET-058's per-channel
history are the SAME code the single-row door runs. **A bulk button is a
different surface, never a different pipeline.**

A refusal the rules make — *"no history — field visit"* — comes back as a
named row beside the estimates, never as a silent skip.

`POST /reads/bulk-fix` — accept a SET of flagged reads, ONE reason.

PO verbatim, 2026-08-26: *"We will need bulk operation"*, and on the
accountability half: *"keep the rule — speed comes from the bulk button…
an auditor asking 'who chose to estimate M-4412?' gets a name"*. Every row
this writes carries `fixed_by`, `fix_reason` and its own `audit_log` row —
there is no anonymous bulk statement anywhere behind this route.

**BR-MET-129 bounds what it can do:** a warned reading already POSTED and
stays posted. This records a judgment after commit (clause 3); it neither
posts a reading nor holds one out, and no error is ever cleared by it —
an error still refuses at import (BR-MET-015's surviving half).

A partly-refused selection answers **200 with per-row outcomes**, not a
4xx: thirty-eight accepted and two explained is the honest result of the
click, and failing all forty over two would be worse for the clerk and
less true.

Estimate ONE missing (meter, channel) record (BR-MET-026/058/062). A
refusal comes back as data with its reason — "no history — field visit" is
an answer the clerk must see, not a 500.

get.description:
S25's landing tab (BR-MET-060). `missing` is the REAL BR-MET-049 count
since CR-038 W1 (US-MET-018): missing required records — meter × channel —
across the active cycles whose read window is OPEN (BR-MET-057). This
docstring said "is not built" and the payload said `missing: null` with a
reason from W2 until 2026-08-26; both statements retired together with the
absence they described. `missing_unresolved_meters` rides along so a small
count over unresolvable meters never reads as "all clear".

`GET reads/photos/{photo_id}/content` — a photograph answer's bytes,
same-origin (`DEF-WRK-9594`'s reason), never kept by a shared cache.

`GET /reads/quick-context` — what the quick-entry MODAL must know first.

PO verbatim, 2026-08-26: *"we will need modpage to load single reading, if
it is simple then modal"*. A modal is sanctioned *if it is simple*, and
**whether this meter is simple is a question only the server can answer** —
it depends on the plan-driven expected register set (BR-MET-049), which
lives in `completeness.PlanRegisterResolver`.

So this read answers three things, and the modal cannot be honest without
any of them:

  1. **The meter**, resolved by number or id within this tenant, with its
     own UoM (hard rule 3 — the modal shows the unit, never guesses it).
  2. **Its registers.** One expected channel → the modal is the right
     surface. Several (a TOU or demand meter) → `simple: false` and the
     modal HANDS OFF to the full manual entry path rather than growing rows
     inside itself. That is the *"if it is simple"* boundary, applied per
     meter, exactly as CR-038's task 6 words it.
  3. **The cycle and period the read will land in** — DERIVED from the read
     date and the meter's own cycle assignment, per CR-038's period/cycle
     sanity statement clause 4: *"the quick single-read modal DERIVES cycle
     + period from the read date and the meter's cycle assignment and SHOWS
     them (the clerk confirms, never types)"*.

⚠ **IT WRITES NOTHING.** A GET that stages a batch is a GET that surprises
somebody. The reading is staged, validated and posted by the SAME three
`/read-batches` routes a CSV uses — this route only tells the modal what to
draw before the clerk commits.

`GET /reads/read-methods` - the tenant's read-method vocabulary.

BR-MET-123 (PO 2026-08-26) makes the read SOURCE a TAG chosen at upload,
and the words are the tenant's own `read_methods` reference list
(BR-AST-043). S28 is the Billing Clerk's screen (BR-MET-035) and
`/lookups/read_methods` is System-Admin-only (DEF-196), so the wizard could
not read the list through Settings - a clerk would have got an empty
control, which is the exact shape of the omission the S28 step-1 panel
already reports about the service tag.

READ-ONLY, and the tenant-scoped role gate is the whole authorisation: this
endpoint lists names a clerk must be able to choose between, and writing to
the list stays where BR-TEN-036 put it - Settings, System Admin only.

`reads_template.csv` — the PUBLISHED standard template (BR-MET-032).
One template, downloadable, re-detected on every upload; there is no
per-tenant variant to serve.

⚠ **`?shape=` PICKS WHICH WORKED EXAMPLE — `CR-077`'s reading starters.**
There is still ONE template: the header row and the mapping are the same
file for all four, which is what BR-MET-032 means by *"exactly one
published template"*. What differs is the worked ROWS, because a read
shape is a file LAYOUT — one row for flat and tiered, three for time of
use, two for demand (energy + peak) and two for net metering (energy +
export). `read_import.READ_SHAPES` carries the four and says why seasonal
is not a fifth.

⚠ **NO `shape` STILL SERVES THE EXACT BYTES IT ALWAYS DID**, and that is a
compatibility promise rather than a default worth defending: this URL has
handed out the demand pair since CR-038 W4, the spec and the front end
name `reads_template.csv`, and changing what an unchanged address serves is
how a bookmark starts lying. Every control on S28 passes a shape, so a
clerk always chooses.

⚠ **AN UNKNOWN SHAPE IS REFUSED BY NAME, NEVER FOLDED TO THE FIRST ONE**
(`sample_csv`'s posture for an unknown target). The message key is
`metering.import.kind_unknown` — *"Pick one of: {{allowed}}."* — REUSED
rather than minted in eleven catalogues for a query parameter, which is the
reuse `_reading_month` above records two routes down and for the same
reason.

S29 — the read, its FULL supersession chain and any J6 correction
linkage opened against it (BR-MET-056 · US-MET-016).

post.description:
US-MET-016: the J6 route — the ONLY door a BILLED read's correction has.

Distinct from `/supersede` on purpose. The plain path REFUSES a billed read
(TC-4) and this one refuses an unbilled one, so neither can be reached by
accident and the routing is visible in the URL a reviewer reads. The
response carries the superseding read AND the `read_corrections` linkage
billing consumes; the invoice itself is untouched (J6 step 1).

S29 Dispute (US-MET-013 TC-3 · BR-MET-024 · the OQ-043 closure).

**THE DOOR DEF-046 SAID DID NOT EXIST.** Its first finding, verbatim:
*"meter_reads carries disputed_at/dispute_reason/disputed_by,
needs_attention_counts COUNTS disputes, and NO service or route ever sets
one -- the chip can only ever read zero."* This is that route.

Records a marker + reason. Changes no value: the correction paths are
`/supersede` (unbilled) and `/billed-correction` (billed), and neither is
reachable from here — a dispute is a claim ABOUT a reading, not a change to
one, and conflating them would let a dispute edit a billed number without
the J6 linkage BR-MET-053 requires.

The account is held from the bill run from this moment until a System Admin
clears it (`/dispute/clear`). Where the read is already BILLED, the response
carries `billed_bill_effect` = `issued_bill_stands_br_met_133`.

⚠ **THIS PARAGRAPH SAID "naming OQ-245 — the issued bill is untouched and
nothing signs what it should do" UNTIL 2026-08-26.** BR-MET-133 signs it:
the bill STANDS (it is not voided and not held — hard rule 4), resolution
goes through the billed-correction door, and while the dispute is open the
DISPUTED AMOUNT does not age into late fees while the undisputed remainder
ages normally.

Clear the dispute and release the account back into the bill run.

System Admin only, by the OQ-043 closure. An optional `resolution` note
rides into the audit row — `meter_reads` has no cleared-reason column (B2
r8) and inventing one is a story's job.

S29 Override = SUPERSEDE (BR-MET-024/053). A billed read is refused —
its correction routes through J6 (US-MET-016), which billing owns.

get.description:
`GET /refunds` — J15 step 2's approval queue, and the refund history.

`?f.status=requested` is what an Admin approves from; no filter is the
reported history. An unknown status is refused with the closed set rather
than answering an empty queue — **an empty queue and an unanswerable one
look identical on a screen** (`write_off_queue`'s own words, and the same
trap).

⚠ **IT PAGES IN SQL SINCE 2026-09-24 (`DEF-PAY-6555` · `NFR-3` · `P1.3`),
AND THIS DOCSTRING CARRIED THE OPPOSITE AS A DECISION.** It read
*"Unpaginated, deliberately: a page of an approval queue is a queue that
lies about what is pending."* The argument is good and the ceiling under it
moved to 40,000 accounts on 2026-09-06. It is ANSWERED rather than
overruled: `count` is the total over the FILTERED set and rides on every
page, so the screen always knows what is pending. Full reasoning in
`selectors.refund_queue`; the judgment is in
`12-governance/02-decision-log.md` under 2026-09-24.

⚠ **BOTH APPROVAL ACTS ARE RENDERED SEPARATELY** and neither is folded into
a boolean — `BR-PAY-037` lets one user initiate and approve in v1 *"as long
as both acts are recorded separately"*, so a row showing only "approved"
would erase the control the rule leans on.

A READ — no audit row.

`GET /refunds-and-credits` — everything this utility has given back.

Screen 6·1's question: *"what have we given back, and can I still tell a
cheque from a credit?"* A clerk closing an account in credit chooses
between a refund and a credit note, and until now the two lived in two
modules with no list that showed both.

⚠ **IT IS A SECOND ROUTE AND NOT A WIDENING OF `GET /refunds`, DELIBERATELY.**
That route is the APPROVAL QUEUE. Its own docstring says it is unpaginated
*because* *"a page of an approval queue is a queue that lies about what is
pending"* — so putting credit notes into it would page it, or would build
every refund the tenant has, and the two questions are different anyway:
one asks *what needs my signature*, this asks *what have we given back*.

**PAGED, `?page` AND `?per`** — `NFR-3`. The page is taken in SQL on BOTH
sides of the module boundary; see `refunds_and_credits.page` for why a
federated page is what a `UNION` cannot be when one table belongs to
billing (B1, B2 §2).

`?f.kind=refund|credit_note` narrows to one source and an unknown value is
REFUSED with the closed set rather than answering an empty list — **an
empty list and an unanswerable one look identical on a screen**
(`refund_queue`'s own recorded trap).

⚠ **`count` IS A TOTAL AND SAYS WHEN IT IS NOT.** If billing publishes no
credit-note read, the envelope carries `credit_notes_read_unavailable` and
the count counts refunds only, in words. A short list with no number
attached to what it left out is `G32`'s defect: a true zero over a scope it
silently excluded.

A READ. No clock, no write, no audit row.

`GET /refunds/{id}` — **the answer to *"where is my money?"*** (P4.4).

╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  A RAISE MODAL AND AN ACT MODAL, AND NOTHING BETWEEN THEM.           ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
`RefundsPage.tsx` could open a form to CREATE a refund and a form to ACT on
one, and there was no way to open a refund and simply LOOK at it. So the
question a customer actually asks on the telephone — *"you said you were
sending my $57.13, where is it?"* — had no screen and no endpoint behind
one. The four act routes below each return the row as a by-product of
changing it; **none of them could be called to find out.**

**THIN BY LAW, AND THE ROW IS THE SAME ROW.** The read is
`selectors.refund_detail`, which already existed and which the approve,
issue, clear and void routes all answer with. No second serialisation of a
money row is added here — `DEF-014`'s exact shape — so a refund cannot look
like one thing after an act and another when opened.

**WHY `AdminOrClerk` AND NOT NARROWER.** `GET /refunds` lists this very row
to the same audience, and `POST /accounts/{id}/refunds` lets that audience
raise one. **A door must not deny a reach its siblings grant** — the
argument `credit_notes_api` records in the other direction — and hiding the
detail of a row already on the clerk's list would be a gate that protects
nothing and teaches the clerk the screen is broken.

⚠ **404-NEVER-403 FOR ANOTHER TENANT'S REFUND.** The selector filters on
the tenant id and a miss is a miss (hard rule 1, `BR-TEN-003`, HR-1). A 403
would confirm the row exists, which is the one thing a stranger must not
learn from a refusal.

**BOTH APPROVAL ACTS STAY SEPARATE ON THE ROW** — `requested_by` and
`approved_by` are distinct members and neither is folded into a boolean,
because `BR-PAY-037` lets one user initiate AND approve in v1 *"as long as
both acts are recorded separately"*, and a detail view showing only
*approved* would erase the control the rule leans on.

A READ. No clock, no money arithmetic, no write, no audit row.

post.description:
`POST /refunds/{id}/approve` — J15 step 3. `BR-PAY-014`'s Admin approval.

**Approval gates the money exactly once**: only a `requested` refund can be
approved and the service refuses every other status by name. It moves no
money — `issue_refund` is the step that draws the customer-credit account
down, and it is a different act.

`approved_at` is the caller's business moment and is **not defaulted to
now**: approval is the control `BR-PAY-014` rests on, and a timestamp the
server invented is a control nobody can reconstruct in a year (hard rule 7).

⚠ **`BR-PAY-037` IS EXERCISED, NOT WORKED AROUND.** The same user holding
the approver role MAY approve their own request in v1 — J15 step 3 is
exactly that — and the control is that BOTH acts are recorded distinctly,
which is why `requested_by_id` and `approved_by_id` are separate columns
rather than a flag. Enforced separation of duties is v2 and nothing here
pre-empts it.

`POST /refunds/{id}/clear` — the cheque cleared the bank (TC-3).

**A status move and a date. It posts NOTHING.** The money left the books at
issue, and posting again on clearing would take it out twice — the service
asserts that and so does `test_us_pay_011_tc3_tc4`, by counting journal
entries either side. What clearing gives is the date bank reconciliation
matches the outgoing item on.

**Admin or Executive** (`BR-PAY-1071`), because CS-6 puts it in one line:
*"it is a bank fact, not an approval"*. A4 gives the finance/reconcile
column to the Executive, and every deposit-batch and bank-statement route in
this module is already `AdminOrExecutive`; gating this one to Admin alone
would mean the person reconciling the bank cannot record that a cheque they
can see on the statement has cleared. A **Billing Clerk is refused**, which
is narrower than yesterday, when this service accepted anybody at all.

⚠ **CS-15 (task 47) IS WHAT LINKS THIS TO ITS BANK LINE**, and it is not
built: outgoing items are not matched against a statement yet, so this
records the fact a person read off the bank's own statement. CS-6's screen
note says the same — the control lives on **S39 beside the bank line** when
CS-15 exists, and on **S58** until then.

`POST /refunds/{id}/correct-reference` — S58's *Correct check number*.

**THE ROUTE IS THE SPEC, as it is for the payment door it mirrors**
(`POST /payments/{id}/correct-reference`, `OQ-1322`): one named verb, and
no PATCH, PUT or DELETE added to any refund path. What may be corrected is
visible here — the body is the whole of it:

    reference   the check number printed on the check — REQUIRED
    note        why it is being corrected — REQUIRED

**Anything else is refused BY NAME** — `amount`, `account_id`, `method`,
and also `memo` and `tender_id`, which the PAYMENT door accepts: the PO was
shown a refund's CHECK NUMBER and nothing else (`OQ-PAY-12614`, PO
2026-09-23, *"(b) Allow a correction, the same way you allowed it for
payments on 2 September"*), so nothing else is signed.

**Admin or Billing Clerk**, mirroring `refunds.correct_refund_reference`'s
service gate and never widening it (BR-SHL-025): the person who writes the
check corrects its number (`BR-PAY-1071` as amended 2026-09-03). An
Executive is refused at both layers.

⚠ **THE ANSWER CARRIES THE STORED ROW, NOT THE SENT VALUE,** and an
`unavailable[]` entry saying the replaced number lives only in `audit_log`,
which is pruned on its one schedule (`OQ-1340`). That entry is a machine
fact for a caller and never copy for a screen — B14 rule 33.

`POST /refunds/{id}/issue` — J15 step 4. **THE MONEY LEAVES HERE.**

`BR-PAY-014`'s posting, and the only step in the refund lifecycle that
moves a cent: DR **2400 Customer credit** / CR **1000 Cash**, composed by
`ledger_seam.post_refund_executed` and written by the ledger posting service
alone (hard rule 5). `PE-9`, exactly: a credit of **57.13** on `ACC-1042`
refunded by cheque **#10241** takes the credit to **0.00**.

**THE CREDIT IS TESTED AGAIN HERE, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF A SEPARATE
STEP.** `_credit_or_refuse` ran at request and runs again at issue, because
an approval given on Tuesday must not pay out a credit that a Wednesday
bounce pulled back — *"a credit real on Tuesday can be gone by Thursday, and
the money moves on Thursday"* (CS-6). The response therefore carries
`credit_position_after` on every step, so the screen never has to remember a
figure it was shown earlier.

`issued_at` is the caller's business moment and is **not defaulted to now**
(BR-TEN-043, gate G6): the day a refund left decides which accounting period
it left in, and a server that read its own clock would let request latency
make that choice.

⚠ **`reference` — THE CHEQUE NUMBER — IS COLLECTED HERE FROM 2026-09-23
(`DEF-PAY-6331`).** It used to be collected on the RAISE form, days before
Finance approves anything and before a cheque exists, and the column was
frozen from row creation — so when the real cheque was written there was
**nowhere in the product to record its number**. The blueprint draws it on
this act and says why in four words: *"the only record of which cheque this
was"* (`06 Payments Page Blueprint.pdf` p078, annotation ②).

It is written in the SAME statement as the status move, inside the same
transaction as the posting and the audit row. ~~and never patched
afterwards~~ — **amended 2026-09-23 (`CR-141-BRC07`, PO ruling
`OQ-PAY-12614`):** issuing still never overwrites a number the row already
holds, and `payments/0041` + `payments/0043` refuse every other rewrite at
the database; a number KEYED wrongly is replaced only through
`POST /refunds/{id}/correct-reference` below. `issue_refund` refuses an
overwrite in Python as well, because the test database is SQLite and has no
triggers (hard-won law 14). `POST /accounts/{id}/refunds` now **refuses** a
`reference` by name rather than storing one.

⚠ **ADMIN OR BILLING CLERK, at the door AND in the service** — `BR-PAY-1071`
as AMENDED by the Product Owner on 2026-09-03, verbatim: *"q6 yes Clark can
issue refund"*. **This route read `SystemAdminOnly` for two days** and the
sentence is corrected rather than left to rot (hard-won law 1). The logic is
the PO's own: **the APPROVAL is the control** — `POST /refunds/{id}/approve`
above is still `SystemAdminOnly` and nothing about who authorises money
leaving has moved — and issuing is the clerical act carrying out a decision
an Admin already made. `POST /refunds/{id}/clear` below is untouched at
`AdminOrExecutive`, and voiding stays Admin.

The door still MIRRORS the service and never widens it (BR-SHL-025): an
Executive is refused at both, so a role that cannot issue is never promised
a reach the service denies. See the module docstring for what the gate's
total absence cost before 2026-09-01.

`POST /refunds/{id}/void` — a cheque lost in the post (US-PAY-011 TC-4).

*"Status → Void with reversing posting (credit restored 57.13); new refund
issuable; no row deleted."* Three things follow and the service asserts each:

  * **No row is deleted.** The trigger refuses DELETE in every status; the
    void is a status move plus a NEW mirror entry (hard rule 4).
  * **The credit comes back by exactly what left.** `reverse_refund_entry`
    hands the ledger its own entry with the sides swapped — **nothing
    recomputes the figure**, here or below (hard rule 5).
  * **A new refund is then issuable**, because the credit position is
    computed from rows and a voided refund is excluded from it.

`void_reason` is REQUIRED and is not defaulted: *"a cheque that left the
building and came back is a fact somebody has to be able to reconstruct in a
year"* (the service's own words, hard rule 7). The service refuses a blank.

get.description:
`GET /reports` — the S44 library (US-REP-001).

**This route is contracted by no signed document and is minted here.**
REPORTED: A11 gives `GET /reports/{key}`; 11b §2.11 gives `/reports/schedules`,
`/history`, `/datasets` and `/custom`; none of the five is an index.

It is served rather than compiled into the client for the one reason a
client cannot cover: **which reports THIS deployment can actually produce,
and why not.** Thirteen of the twenty-three cards ship `available: false` today,
each naming the read that would close it — and a card grid drawn from a
hardcoded client list has no way to say so. It would show twenty-three confident
tiles and discover on click that most answer nothing, which is the
"confident empty report" posture S60 was built to avoid.

The vocabularies the S46 parameter bar needs ride along on the same answer
(BR-REP-006 — services are the tenant's ENABLED set, never the prototype's
hardcoded trio), so opening the library costs one request and the parameter
bar cannot render a service the tenant does not have.

`GET /reports/customer-statement?customer={id}` — **CR-060 C16 / T17.**

One customer, their accounts, each balance, **and a total across them**.
**NO MIGRATION AND NO NEW TABLE:** the link table has carried the pair, the
confidence tier and the confirmer since `BR-CUS-054` shipped, and every
money figure is the ledger's own per-account Σ reached through the customers
seam. This view adds a door, not a derivation.

**WHY IT LIVES IN CUSTOMERS AND NOT IN REPORTS.** The read walks
`customer_accounts` — a customers table — and B1 forbids another module
touching this one's ORM. The `reports/` PREFIX is the URL grammar for a
report and is not a claim about ownership; `apps/audit/api.py` already
serves `reports/user-activity-audit` on exactly that reading.

**THE CUSTOMER IS A QUERY PARAMETER, NOT A PATH SEGMENT**, because the URL
is a REPORT's and a report is parameterised. A missing or malformed
`customer` is a 422 rather than a 404: *"you did not say who"* and *"there
is no such person"* are different answers, and collapsing them would send a
clerk looking for a deleted customer who never existed.

404-never-403 for an id another tenant holds (HR-1/G4): from outside the
tenant an id that exists elsewhere and one that does not are the same fact,
and telling them apart is a membership oracle.

A READ — no audit row (CLAUDE.md rule 7 is about money ACTIONS).

`GET /reports/dashboard` — screen `3·1`.

Reads nothing from the caller but the two controls the drawing has (p36 ③:
*"Set the period · set what to compare it against · open a panel. That is
the whole surface"*), and **writes nothing at all** (p36 ④, p38 ⓸ — *"No
write of any kind, not even a remembered period"*).

`GET /reports/datasets` (11b §2.11) — `P0.4`'s metadata endpoint.

Serves the DECLARATION in `apps/reports/datasets.py`: nine datasets, each
with its grain, its columns with a type — and, where a column is a
quantity, its unit (CLAUDE.md hard rule 3) — its measures with an
aggregation AND an additivity (`P0.16`), its dimensions with attributes and
hierarchies, and the filters it accepts.

It is served rather than compiled into the client for BR-REP-006's reason,
the same one `report_library` gives: a vocabulary is read LIVE, never
hardcoded into a screen. The edit panel says *"13 available"* and *"4 of 7
shown"* by counting what is here, so a screen and the engine cannot be
counting different things — which is exactly what the six hand-typed maps
`P0.7` deletes were doing.

⚠ **IT IS NOT IN `06-backend/openapi/schema.json` AND THAT IS DELIBERATE
(`DEF-GOV-6800`).** That file is a generated artifact nothing regenerates
or diffs in `run_gates` — hard-won law 1 records that three files describe
an OpenAPI CI-diff no workflow runs, and that is still true. Measured on
2026-09-26 it is **six routes behind the code before this one**, all six
other lanes'. Regenerating is a 316 KB whole-file rewrite that would
publish those six under this lane's commit with a correct file count (law
11, mechanism five), so it was not done.

⚠ Three of the nine carry `paginates: false`. That is not a defect in this
payload: `invoices`, `payments` and `journal_lines` do not accept
`limit`/`offset`/`sort` in their owning modules today (`DEF-PAY-4221`), and
those three feed 32 of the 46 definitions. Serving `true` would be a check
that cannot fail.

post.description:
`POST /reports/definitions` — screen 2·4's **Save as** (`P5.1`).

⚠ **THE REPLY IS 201 AND IT CARRIES THE KEY, BECAUSE THE SCREEN NAVIGATES.**
p23's DOORS row: *"the confirmation after Save as: saving a report drops you
here with it in view, because a save that gives no sign of where the thing
went is how a clerk saves the same report three times."* A body without the
key would make the screen guess the address from the name, and the slug is
this server's to compute — `Overdue 60+` twice gives `overdue-60` and
`overdue-60-2`, and only the server knows which one it just wrote.

⚠ **`tenant_id` IS NOT ACCEPTED AND NEVER WILL BE.** Hard rule 1: the tenant
comes from the request context. A tenant id in a body is a tenant id a
caller can edit.

delete.description:
`PATCH`/`DELETE /reports/definitions/{id}` — 2·2's save, and 1·2's delete.

⚠ **A PLATFORM ROW REACHED HERE IS REFUSED, NOT COPIED.** Copy-on-write
lives on the POST: a screen editing a built-in has never owned a row to
PATCH, so it calls Save as. If an id for one of the forty-six arrives here
it is a client bug, and answering it by quietly creating a different row
would hide that bug behind a success.

patch.description:
`PATCH`/`DELETE /reports/definitions/{id}` — 2·2's save, and 1·2's delete.

⚠ **A PLATFORM ROW REACHED HERE IS REFUSED, NOT COPIED.** Copy-on-write
lives on the POST: a screen editing a built-in has never owned a row to
PATCH, so it calls Save as. If an id for one of the forty-six arrives here
it is a client bug, and answering it by quietly creating a different row
would hide that bug behind a success.

get.description:
`GET /reports/history` — screen `5·1`'s rows (`CR-142-BRC07` `P3.1`).

⚠ **PAGED, ALWAYS, AND THE PAGE IS CUT IN SQL** (`NFR-3`). `DEF-PAY-4221`
is the register row for the four reads in this product that are not, and
the reason this one never joins them is that a run history only grows: a
utility at the top of the ICP running four reports a day on a schedule
writes ~1,460 rows a year and nothing ever deletes one.

⚠ **THE PARAMS ARE THE KIT'S OWN NAMES** — `q`, `page`, `per`, plus
`f.report` and `f.status` — so `DataTable` drives this endpoint with the
request state it already builds for every other list. A filter naming a
report this module does not own is IGNORED rather than refused: the value
comes from a select whose options this same endpoint publishes, so a bad
one is a stale tab rather than a caller error, and an empty page is the
honest answer to it.

`GET /reports/history/{job_id}` — screen `5·2`, one run opened.

Absent, malformed, another tenant's, or a job that is not a REPORT run →
the same plain 404 (HR-1 / 11b G4: existence must not leak, and a
distinguishable message would confirm the id).

`GET /reports/schedules` — `4·1`'s rows · `POST` — `2·3` commits.

⚠ **PAGED, ALWAYS, AND CUT IN SQL** (`NFR-3`). Four rows today need no
pager and get one anyway: `P4.5`'s own ⚠ — *"rule 16 has no small-list
exemption, and a utility with forty schedules is the case it is for."*

post.description:
`POST /reports/schedules/{id}/run-now` — `4·1`'s ▶ row action.

⚠ **IT DOES NOT ADVANCE `next_run_at`** (p41 ④, verbatim: *"Run now writes
a job row, which appears on `5·1` within a second and produces a file — ⚠
it does NOT advance `next_run_at`, so the scheduled run still happens."*)
A clerk checking that a schedule works must not thereby cancel Monday's run.

⚠ **AND ITS SCOPE KEY CARRIES THE MOMENT, NOT THE DUE DATE**, so pressing
▶ twice deliberately produces two files while the SWEEP still folds. Two
people pressing it in the same second is the one case that folds, which is
the right answer for that case too.

get.description:
`GET` the tenant's service accounts · `POST` issues one.

⚠ **THE TOKEN IS IN THE `POST` ANSWER AND IN NO OTHER ANSWER, EVER.** There
is no read that can return it, by construction: only the hash is stored.
The `GET` carries `token_prefix` so an administrator can tell two apart.

post.description:

The `GET` carries `token_prefix` so an administrator can tell two apart.

`POST /reports/service-accounts/{id}/revoke` — stop it, keep its history.

⚠ **A TIMESTAMP AND NOT A DELETE.** §7.8: *"a revoked account silently
breaks a board pack"* is a thing somebody has to be able to look up
afterwards, and a deleted row takes its own trail with it. Revoking twice is
idempotent and keeps the FIRST timestamp — the second call is somebody
making sure, not a new fact.

get.description:
`GET /reports/{key}` (11b §1 · 13a) — S59 and S60 today.

⚠ **`P5.9` — A KEY THIS ROLE MAY NOT RUN IS `403 AUTH-002`, NOT 404 AND NOT
AN EMPTY RESULT.** `BR-REP-023` restricts `access_review` to System Admin
and Executive; the floor lives on the DEFINITION (`min_role`) and is read
by `apps/reports/role_gate.py`, the same function the catalogue asks — so a
card that is absent for this role and an address that serves it cannot
disagree. A 404 would make a restricted report indistinguishable from a
typo, and `HR-1` reserves 404 for another tenant's resource.

An unknown key is **VAL-005 BIZ-free 422**, carrying the served vocabulary
in `params.keys`. Two alternatives were rejected: a 404 (which would make
an unbuilt report indistinguishable from a typo, and from another tenant's
resource — the one thing HR-1 reserves 404 for) and a silent empty result
(a report viewer that renders nothing for `?key=revenue_by_srevice` is the
hardest bug in this product to see).

GET /retention/runs — **has the retention job ever run, and what moved?**

US-MET-020 / US-AUD-007's run record, reachable for the first time. Its
`archive_job_runs` ledger has existed since audit migration 0004, is written
on every run by `core.archival` through a registered recorder, and appeared
in a migration, a management command and `core/archival.py` **and in no
`api.py` anywhere**. An operator subject to a 7-year retention obligation
could not answer the question at all.

**READ-ONLY BY CONSTRUCTION, and here that is a rule rather than a habit.**
BR-MET-055 and BR-AUD-012 both say archival is *"an AUTOMATIC scheduled job
… never manual"*, and `core.archival.run_archival` refuses any caller
without the scheduler token `manage.py archive_partitions` holds. This class
defines `get` and nothing else, so POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE answer 405 from
DRF's own dispatch — the same structural refusal `AuditLogView` relies on
(BR-AUD-002 / HR-4). Making the job triggerable from here would be building
exactly the product path both rules forbid.

ROLE GATE: the same `AdminOrExecutive` the rest of this module carries
(BR-AUD-009). Retention is a compliance read over the same store.

⚠ **`archive_job_runs` HAS NO `tenant_id` AND NO RLS POLICY** — a partition
is shared across tenants, so a run belongs to none of them. The selector
REDACTS each entry's tenant list to a single "were my rows in this one?"
boolean before it leaves the module; nothing here serves the raw payload,
because on this one table RLS has no policy to catch a leak with.

`GET /returned-mail` — the needs-attention list (J18 step 5).

Oldest first, always: *"2 open needs-attention rows that will age visibly —
the queue never silently drops them."* There is no sort control because the
order IS the rule. The page is a `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` over payments' own table
and the three enrichment reads are taken once for the page.

post.description:
`POST /returned-mail/clear` — the address was dealt with; bring the flag down.

`resolution` is `address_corrected` (the clerk used the owning module's
address door first) or `verified_current` (the address was right and the
carrier was wrong). `resolved_on` is the business date the clerk types.

get.description:
SET-06 step 3 — the meters the chosen premises bring (BR-MET-075).

⚠ **`unit_id` IS GONE AND `premises_id` REPLACES IT (`CR-131-BRC07`).** The
wizard sent one `unit_id` per unit: **37,994 characters at 726 units**
against a 4–8 KB limit, so the request never arrived and step 3 drew its
empty state over a route full of meters. A saved route now sends nothing
but `route_id`; an open wizard sends the **6** premises it has ticked.

⚠ **A `unit_id` PARAMETER IS NOT SILENTLY IGNORED — it is REFUSED BY
NAME.** Accepting and dropping it would give a caller that had not been
updated an empty meter list and no reason, which is the same false absence
the whole of this change exists to remove. `BR-SHL`'s posture: a request
this endpoint cannot honour says so.

BR-MET-073 — the code SET-06 step 1 pre-fills, EDITABLE. A preview, so
opening the wizard and cancelling does not burn a number.

SET-06 step 2 — the dual-pane picker's left side (BR-MET-072/074).

`area` repeats for a multi-select (`?area=NORTH&area=SOUTH`), which is
how the "1 to many" ruling reaches the wire; absent = All.

⚠ **IT ANSWERS THE `{count, results}` ENVELOPE AND IT PAGES SERVER-SIDE
(`DEF-MET-5743`, `NFR-3`).** It served a BARE ARRAY of every matching
premises in the tenant until 2026-09-18, built with one `Unit` query and
one `assets_on_unit` call per row — correct at the <3,000-connection
ceiling this product was scoped to until 2026-09-06, and 13× short of T5's
40,000. The PO's own words for what it cost: *"Route setup becomes
unusable at 5,000–10,000 premises"*.

⚠ **AND `per` CARRIES NO MAXIMUM (`NFR-5`).** Omitting it still returns
every matching row, so nothing here is a cap that would have to be removed
when T4 arrives; what is added is the ABILITY to ask for a window and be
told the true total beside it. The screen asks for one; an export or a
test may still ask for all of them.

`sort`/`dir` are `BR-SHL-011`'s grammar, over the vocabulary
`selectors.PREMISES_PICKER_SORTS` declares — an unknown key falls back to
the default rather than erroring, as `/routes` and `/cycles` already do.

`members=1` narrows to the premises already on `route_id`. That is the
EDIT path: re-opening a route must re-tick its own members, and with a
paged picker those rows are mostly not on the page in front of you. It is
bounded by the route rather than by the tenant (`BR-MET-055`).

post.description:
MQ-033 (PO 2026-10-24) — set or clear the reader on one or many routes,
from Reads → cycle → Routes: `{"route_ids": [...], "reader_id": <uuid>|null}`.

⚠ **OFFICE ROLES THAT DO THE DAY'S WORK — ADMIN AND CLERK.** Who walks a
route this month is reading WORK, which `BR-MET-011` as narrowed makes
writable on the Reads screen; the route's DEFINITION stays System Admin's
in Settings. An executive reads; a field technician never reaches this.
The service is `route_readers.set_reader` and its docstring says what it
refuses and why.

get.description:
MQ-033 — the reader picker: this tenant's ACTIVE field technicians,
`?q=` matching name or email, paged in SQL (NFR-3, nothing capped).

SET-06D's **Accounts** tab — *"the accounts a missed read here affects"*.

⚠ **STATUS ONLY (D12, *"not required"*).** The screenshot draws a Balance
column; routes and cycles are grouping only (BR-MET-078, hardened by this
CR), so no money reaches this payload — asserted by test, not by eye.

The accounts come through the reviewed customers seam
(`apps/metering/seams.py`), one batched read for the whole route rather
than `GET /accounts?unit_id=` once per unit (D7).

put.description:
CR-029 D3 + D11 — **the walking order, per premises**.

SET-06D's drag-to-reorder has POSTed here since it shipped and got a 404,
because RC-W1 landed `route_premises_orders` and mounted no path (B17 §5
gap G5: *"exists with a uniqueness constraint and NO WRITER"*). This is
the door.

The body is `{"order": [{"premises_id": …, "walk_order": N}, …]}` — what
`walkOrderPayload()` already sends — and a bare list of premises ids is
accepted too, position first. The whole walk travels: a list that omits or
repeats a member is refused before anything is written.

⚠ **PUT ONLY, AND THE MISSING GET IS DELIBERATE.** `GET /routes/{id}`
already serves `premises_order`, so a second read of the same fact would be
a route with no caller — the mirror of the defect this wave exists to fix
(hard-won law 2), and a second place for the stop list to be right or wrong.

get.description:
CR-029 D1 — SET-06D's **Read history**: Window · Read on · Reader ·
Collected · Expected · Result, newest walk first.

`read_windows` became a first-class closable record in RC-W1-T4 and RC-W2
wrote the closer; nothing served the rows, so the Audit tab said so rather
than drawing six empty columns. `limit` clamps into 1…200 (BR-SHL-011's
never-error posture) and defaults to 50, the one page size this product
already uses everywhere.

── W5-T6 ASKED WHETHER THIS JOINS THE PAGED GRAMMAR. IT DOES NOT. ────────
B17 §7 W5-T6 leaves the choice open and asks for the answer to be stated,
so: **`limit`, no `page`, and this is a bounded HISTORY rather than a
list.** Three reasons, none of them "later".

  1. There is no pager on the surface. SET-06D's Read history is a card
     inside a tab that renders the most recent walks; a `{count, next}`
     envelope would describe navigation no control offers, which is
     hard-won law 2 (a payload no screen reads).
  2. `count` would cost a second query per open of the tab to answer a
     question nobody asks. The rows are answered newest-first and the
     honest claim is *"the last N"*, which `limit` states exactly.
  3. Page 2 of a history that grows at the top is not stable. A crew
     closing a window between two requests shifts every row down one, so a
     paged read history serves duplicates and skips — the same reason
     `GET /billing/runs` keeps this posture.

If a screen ever needs to walk the whole history, that is a different
endpoint shape (a keyset cursor on `period_start`), not this one with a
`page` param bolted on.

CR-038 W5 — the RDS-01 header button, finally live: the printable route
sheet, served as PRINT-READY HTML (a self-contained page with its own
@media print stylesheet).

NOT PDF bytes, and that is a recorded lane decision, not an oversight: no
PDF library is a backend dependency, adding one is not a lane's call, and
the one hand-rolled PDF writer in the product is billing's own module
scoped to the bill document (see apps/metering/route_sheet.py's docstring).
The browser's Print / Save as PDF is the "PDF" the r10 button promises.

Opens in its own tab from S25 (the same same-origin-anchor pattern the
bill's `/document.pdf` uses), so the session cookie rides along and HR-1's
one 404 covers an unknown, malformed or cross-tenant route id.

`GET /runbooks` — row 1 · `POST /runbooks` — row 5. One address, two verbs.

**GET** serves `RBS-001` (Runbooks home) and `RBS-003` (My runbooks). Pages
server-side with `per` clamped 50/100/200/500/1000, default 50 (`NFR-3`),
and carries no per-tenant maximum of any kind (`NFR-5`) — a tenant with four
hundred cloned runbooks gets four hundred, fifty at a time. From wave `D5`
it is narrowed by **role visibility** (`RB-050`, `BR-RBS-024` clause 2):
what a signed-in staff member is SHOWN, never what they may call.

**POST** adds a shipped template to My runbooks — `07-endpoints.md` row 5,
body `{template_key}`, **Admin**, `201 · the new runbook`. `BR-RBS-043`:
add once, then clone; a second add is refused rather than answered `201`
over a row that already existed.

⚠ **`POST` LANDS ON THIS FUNCTION BECAUSE DJANGO TAKES THE FIRST PATTERN
THAT MATCHES AND `runbooks` IS ONE ADDRESS.** A second view mounted on the
same path would never be reached — which is `integrations/subprocessors`'
defect wearing a different hat. The permission split is in the class, never
in an `if` here (`DEF-196`).

`GET /runbooks` — row 1 · `POST /runbooks` — row 5. One address, two verbs.

**GET** serves `RBS-001` (Runbooks home) and `RBS-003` (My runbooks). Pages
server-side with `per` clamped 50/100/200/500/1000, default 50 (`NFR-3`),

get.description:
`GET /runbooks/runs` — row 8: history across runbooks, newest first.

`RBS-008`. Filters are `BR-SHL-011`'s `f.<name>` grammar: `f.runbook`,
`f.category`, `f.kind`, `f.outcome`, `f.from`, `f.to`. An unknown filter
name is IGNORED and an unknown value falls back to unfiltered — a list URL
never 4xx's over its own params.

`GET /runbooks/runs/{id}` — row 9: header, counts, status, approver.

⚠ **A RUN OF ANOTHER TENANT AND A RUN THAT NEVER EXISTED ANSWER THE SAME
404** (`HR-1`, hard rule 1). The read is filtered by tenant BEFORE the id is
looked at, so neither the status nor the body can be used to ask whether a
given run id is real somewhere else in the product.

`GET /runbooks/runs/{id}/records` — row 11: the plan and the outcome.

Filter with `f.outcome`. Paged like every other list here; a volume runbook
writes a record row only for what it acted on or flagged and a COUNT per
outcome for the rest (`BR-RBS-035`), so this list and the run's `counts`
answer two different questions and a screen needs both.

`GET /runbooks/runs/{id}/report` — row 10: **the frozen block list**.

`BR-RBS-020`: *a run's report is composed once, at CLOSE, from the twelve
block types, and frozen; a later code change never alters a past result.*
This route reads `runbook_runs.report` and answers it. It does not call the
runbook's `report()`, does not re-derive a block, does not reshape a
payload, does not add a field a newer renderer wants and does not drop one
it no longer draws.

⚠ **`07-endpoints.md` E-5 NAMES THIS ROUTE AS THE PLACE THE MISTAKE GETS
MADE:** *"a build lane that renders from the live definition instead passes
every test until a runbook is edited, and then rewrites history."* It passes
every test because a fresh fixture's live report and its frozen one are
identical; the difference appears only after an edit, which no fixture
performs by accident. `TC-RBS-16` is the assertion, and this wave's version
of it re-reads the route TWICE and compares the two response bodies BYTE FOR
BYTE.

⚠ **AND IT MATTERS TODAY, NOT ONLY AFTER AN EDIT.** `DEF-RBS-4284` is open:
the engine's six payloads and the wave-C renderer's six types disagree, and
the fix moves the ENGINE onto the renderer's shapes. A run closed before
that lands is frozen in the old shape and one closed after it in the new,
**and both are correct** — the report is what was composed that day. A
serializer that "helped" by translating between them would rewrite the first
result this product ever produced.

The body is `{"blocks": [...]}` rather than a bare array: a top-level JSON
array cannot be extended without breaking every reader, and a run that
failed at close legitimately has **no** blocks — `{"blocks": []}` says that,
where a bare `[]` and a missing response read the same.

`GET …/runs/{id}/results/{done|not-done}.csv` — row 14: the two files.

*Each row carrying its reason and its fix* — `07-endpoints.md` row 14, and
`BR-RBS-011` is why the fix column is not optional: **a failure with no
route is a defect in the runbook**, because a finding a clerk cannot act on
is a finding we should not have shown them.

⚠ **IT STREAMS, AND THAT IS THE `NFR-3`/`NFR-5` ANSWER FOR A DOWNLOAD.** A
file with a page 2 is not a file, so this is the one read in the module that
is deliberately not paged — which is precisely the shape `DEF-PAY-4221`
describes (`GET /outstandings`, unpaginated *"ON PURPOSE … at a utility
under 3,000 connections"*). The difference is that nothing is materialised:
`StreamingHttpResponse` pulls the queryset with an iterator and the peak
memory is one row, whatever the tenant's size. There is no cap on how many
rows the file may carry — only on how many are in memory at once, which is
what `NFR-5` asks for and what an unpaginated `list(...)` does not give.

⛔ **`stream_within_tenant_context` IS NOT DECORATION — `DEF-RBS-4296`, AND
IT IS `DEF-2734` A SECOND TIME.** A `StreamingHttpResponse` returns from the
view with its body UNCONSUMED. `TenantContextMiddleware` clears
`app.tenant_id` in its `finally` the moment the view returns, and the WSGI
server iterates the body afterwards — so the generator's first query runs
with **no tenant marker**, the RLS policy's
`NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid` is NULL,
`tenant_id = NULL` is not TRUE, and the queryset yields **zero rows**.
Nothing raises. The download succeeds with a 200. **The file is a header and
nothing under it**, which reads as *"the run did nothing"* — the most
dangerous shape this product has.

It was written without the wrapper here and the whole SQLite suite was green
over it, because SQLite has no row-level security at all (hard-won law 14).
`tests/test_us_rbs_003_pg.py` caught it on the first PostgreSQL run, and the
case it caught it with asserts a NAMED ROW is in the body rather than
asserting a status — a status assertion passes on an empty file.

A run of another tenant and a run that never existed are the same 404.

`GET /runbooks/templates` — row 4: the shipped library, per tenant.

`RBS-002`. Each row says **Added** or **Not added** for THIS tenant, and
`category_chips` is built from the templates PRESENT and never from the
fixed sixteen (`BR-RBS-025`, `TC-RBS-20`) — a chip that filters to nothing
is dead UI (hard-won law 2).

⚠ **THE CHIPS ARE SPREAD ONTO THE ENVELOPE, NOT RETURNED BESIDE IT.**
`_envelope` builds a fresh dict and discards every other key; a view with an
extra figure that hands its whole result to it loses that figure silently,
which is exactly how `maintenance_index` never left the server
(`DEF-AST-4120`).

`GET /runbooks/{key}` — row 2 · `PUT /runbooks/{key}` — row 3.

`RBS-004.1`, the setup renderer's head.

⚠ **REGISTERED LAST, AND THAT IS WHAT KEEPS `runbooks/templates` AND
`runbooks/runs` REACHABLE.** `<str:key>` matches either of those literals,
and Django takes the FIRST pattern that matches. `integrations/subprocessors`
is the same collision, shipped: read as a provider key and answered 405
under a comment asserting it could not happen. The tests resolve all eight
paths through `config/urls.py` so the ordering is asserted rather than
reasoned about.

⚠ **`schedule.next_run` IS `null` AND IT IS NOT A PLACEHOLDER.** Nothing in
this product schedules a runbook yet: this module registers no job with the
platform runner and `runbooks` carries no `next_run_at` column. `cron` and
`timezone` travel as DECLARED so `RBS-004.3` can draw *"Nightly at 02:00,
America/Chicago"* from the declaration itself; a computed next occurrence
would be this module answering a question no part of it can yet act on, and
`RB-022`'s rule runs both ways — a **Run ▶** a screen offers must actually
run, and a schedule a screen displays must actually fire.

⚠ **`RBS-004.6`'s RUNS TAB IS `GET /runbooks/runs?f.runbook={key}`, NOT A
SECOND PAGE ON THIS ROUTE.** `07-frontend/src/api/runbooksEndpoints.ts`
(wave C task `C3`, written before this endpoint existed) calls
`/runbooks/{key}?runs_page=&runs_per=` and says in its own docstring that it
is *"a claim on `D1`"* to be settled with one mapper if `D1` serves
something else. It does, and the reason is worth a sentence rather than a
parameter: the run history is ALREADY a paged list with a runbook filter
(`07-endpoints.md` row 8), already ordered on a total key, already tested
against 51 rows. A second paging surface on the detail would be the same
list described twice, and two descriptions of one list is `G114`'s whole
subject — three shipped Work screens drew empty tables over exactly that.
So this payload carries the runbook's FACTS and its `last_run` summary; the
Runs tab asks the history route for its page.

⚠ **AND IT DOES NOT SERVE `RunbookSetupView` EITHER, DELIBERATELY.** That
type is a RENDERED view model — translated chrome labels, `SetupValue`
wrappers, one-sentence copy. Serving it from Django would put screen copy in
Python and out of the eleven locale catalogues, which is B14's line and not a
style preference. `contract.py` rules the twelve BLOCK shapes to the
renderer because a block payload is data with no words in it; a setup view
is words. The mapper belongs where `runbooksEndpoints.ts` already put it.

⚠ **`PUT` CHANGES SCHEDULE, CAP, GATE, ENABLED AND VISIBILITY, AND WRITES A
NEW VERSION** — `07-endpoints.md` row 3 plus `RB-050`'s *an Admin may widen
or narrow it per runbook*. `services.update_runbook` holds the whole rule:
an unknown field is refused, a frozen one is refused BY NAME, a no-op edit
writes no version, and an edit to an Action drops the trust ratchet

post.description:
`POST /runbooks/{key}/clone` — row 6: clone and vary (`RB-040`).

Body `{name}`; the copy carries `origin = cloned` and **its own version 1**.
**Admin** · `201 · the copy`. This is wave E's goal sentence: *Tom clones
Dunning, names it Commercial accounts, sets the first reminder to 15 days —
both rows appear with their own schedule, cap and dry run, the Activity tab
names him and the time, and the previous run still reads v3 with its report
unchanged.*

⚠ **THE SOURCE'S OWN RUN HISTORY IS NOT COPIED, AND THAT IS THE SECOND HALF
OF THE GOAL SENTENCE.** *The previous run still reads v3 with its report
unchanged* is a fact about the SOURCE, which this route does not touch at
all: no version of the source is written, no run of the source is altered,
and `runbook_versions` is append-only in the database from `migrations/0003`
so a later lane cannot do it by accident either.

⚠ **REGISTERED BEFORE `runbooks/<str:key>`, LIKE EVERY OTHER LITERAL.** It is
three segments and out of collision range with the two-segment key pattern,
but the ordering rule in this file is *literals first* without exceptions —
an exception is what a later lane copies.

A runbook of another tenant and one that never existed are the same 404
(`HR-1`): the lookup is filtered by tenant before the key is looked at.

get.description:
`GET /runbooks/{key}/domains/{parameter}` — what this tenant may choose.

`BR-RBS-042` clause 2, PO verbatim 2026-09-06: *"every utility will not have
all utility services or all combinations of Plans and rates, so we ahve to
work in variables"*. **A two-service utility's *Services* list offers two.**

⚠ **IT PAGES, AND THE REASON IS THE `account` DOMAIN RATHER THAN THIS
WAVE'S OWN DEMONSTRATION.** `service` is bounded by an eleven-row platform
catalogue and would fit in one response for ever; `account` is **40,000 at
the top of T5** with no ceiling above it (`NFR-5`). CLAUDE.md's opening
paragraph names four shipped lists that are unpaginated *"on purpose"*
because a utility under 3,000 connections could carry it — correct at T7 and
13× short of T5 (`DEF-PAY-4221`). A picker endpoint that paged for one
domain and not another would also be a client that has to know which is
which, so it pages for both.

⚠ **AN EMPTY DOMAIN IS A 200 WITH ZERO ROWS, NEVER A 404 AND NEVER AN
ERROR** (`TC-RBS-039.3`). A utility that has enabled no services yet is a
utility mid-setup, not a bad request; the screen draws a sentence rather
than an empty dropdown, which reads as broken.

⚠ **A PARAMETER WITH NO DOMAIN IS A 404 AND NOT AN EMPTY LIST.** *There is
no list behind this input* and *this input's list is empty* are different
facts, and a screen that could not tell them apart would draw *"you have not
set any services up yet"* over a money box.

get.description:
US-SHL-003 — one grouped, capped, tenant-scoped, role-filtered search.

A4/BR-SHL-025: every signed-in role may search. Finding a record grants
nothing — the record's own endpoint re-checks the caller's role when they
open it, and a search that worked for one role and silently returned less
for another would read as broken data rather than as a permission.

`/service-request-settings/document-requirements` — *"Settings grows a
checklist — for each request type, tick which documents are required."*

⚠ **THE GET RETURNS THE WHOLE GRID, TICKED OR NOT.** A checklist that listed
only what somebody had already touched could never be ticked for the first
time. `configured: false` is how the screen tells *"nobody has looked"* from
*"we said no"*.

⚠ **AND THE SHIPPED ANSWER IS EVERY CELL UNTICKED.** BR-CUS-095's sharpest
clause: *"We ship with nothing ticked, and a utility that configures nothing
blocks nothing."* No pre-tick of `proof_of_identity`, however reasonable it
looks — the product ships with no opinion about any jurisdiction's law.

**System Admin only**: this changes what every future approval of that job
type demands, which is a settings act, not a capture act.

get.description:
`GET /service-requests/capture-defaults` — what a NEW request opens on.

⚠ **THE DATE IS COMPUTED HERE AND NOT IN THE BROWSER, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
REASON THIS ENDPOINT EXISTS.** Fifteen WORKING days means weekends out AND
**this tenant's own public holidays** out (`BR-TEN-039`,
`holiday_calendars`), and the browser holds neither the calendar nor the
tenant's timezone. A front end counting weekdays by itself would answer a
different date from every other business-day figure in this product, wrong
by exactly one day per holiday in the window.

⚠ **IT REUSES `cut_date.business_days_after` AND WRITES NO ARITHMETIC OF ITS
OWN.** That function carries `BR-BIL-002`'s convention — the start day is
never one of the counted days — and `late_fee._business_days_between` shares
it. **Two ways to count working days is two things that can disagree about
when a customer gets service**, so a second counter is not an option.

⚠ **THE CALENDAR IS AN ARGUMENT, NEVER A QUERY INSIDE THE COUNTER**
(`BR-TEN-043`). `seams.tenant_holidays()` is what refuses an unreachable
calendar, and an EMPTY set is a legitimate answer meaning *this utility
keeps no calendar*, never *we could not look*.

**Worked, on the demo tenant, 2026-09-22 (a Tuesday), 22 holiday rows:**
15 working days lands on **2026-10-14**. Without the calendar it would be
2026-10-13 — Columbus Day (2026-10-12) falls inside the window and pushes it
one day, which is the difference this endpoint exists to get right.

`GET /service-requests/categories` — the categories THIS utility uses.

⚠ **IT SERVED SEVEN, FROM A TUPLE, AND SILENTLY DROPPED EVERY ROW A TENANT
ADDED (`DEF-CUS-5647`).** It read the live rows into a dict and then
iterated `AccountType.SEVEN_CATEGORIES` over it, so a row outside that
tuple could not appear however active it was. That was defensible while
`account_types` was a PLATFORM table whose seven codes were a signed
vocabulary; the PO ruling of 2026-09-17 — *"utility can get their own
account types"* — makes it a real bug, and this is the fix. **The picker
now offers every ACTIVE, non-legacy row of this tenant's own list.**

Served as two lists rather than one flag, because the difference is the
whole of `BR-CUS-094`:

  · `selectable` — every active, non-legacy row a new record may pick.
  · `legacy` — `government` on a seeded list, and whatever else a tenant has
    retired from new business. A legacy code **stops being selectable and
    changes nothing else**: still a valid FK, still filterable, still
    priceable, every existing account keeps it and bills exactly as it did.
    Re-pointing it to Municipal or Institutional is a HUMAN act per record,
    because the stored value cannot tell a city water department from a
    state university.

⚠ **THE ORDER IS A STORED FACT NOW, NOT AN ITERATION ORDER.** REQ-03.2 draws
the chips as Residential · Commercial · Industrial · Agricultural ·
Institutional · Municipal · Builder or developer and `BR-CUS-094` lists them
in exactly that order, so sorting by `code` would put Agricultural first and
quietly re-order a screen the PO drew. The seeded seven therefore carry that
order in `account_types.sort_order` as 10..70 (`customers.0054`), the legacy
slot is 900, and **a row the tenant ADDS is appended at `max + 10`** — so
the drawn order survives and new rows land behind it, in the order the
utility created them. `code` is the tiebreak so two rows sharing a slot
still sort deterministically (IS-2).

⚠ **`/lookups/account_types` (the S8 card) now serves `legacy` too**, so a
picker built against either surface can tell a retired code from a live one.

`GET .../applicant-message-templates?occasion=…&search=…` — the picker.

Drawn beneath the block as `Choosing a template`: a search box helped
*"Searches the name a human gave it."* and a table of
`TEMPLATE · GROUP · CHANNEL · VARIANT · VERSION` with a radio per row.

⚠ **A DRAFT ROW IS RETURNED AND MUST BE RENDERED**, disabled, carrying
`pickable: false` and its reason. p081: *"Hiding it sends a clerk looking
for something they can see exists; offering it would queue a letter nobody
has approved."* Filtering it out on the screen is the behaviour that rule
exists to forbid.

`GET|PUT .../applicant-messages` — the drawn `What goes out to the applicant`.

Capture step 6, p080, read as an image: five rows under `SEND · WHAT IT SAYS
· TO · CHANNEL · TEMPLATE · WHEN`, three of them ticked.

**GET** answers the five rows in the drawing's order, whether or not
anything has been stored — the defaults are a constant, so a request nobody
has touched and a request that predates the table both answer correctly
rather than answering empty.

**PUT** stores what the clerk ticked and picked. A row is refused by name
for a template that is not this occasion's, for a DRAFT (p081: *"The draft
version is listed and cannot be picked"*), and for a variant that cannot be
read as writing on the decision row (*"A text never replaces a posted
notice"*).

⚠ **THE PAYLOAD SAYS NOTHING IS SENT AND MEANS IT.** `delivery` carries
`BR-NOT-013` — no provider adapter exists on any channel — so a screen built
on this must say QUEUED and never *sent*. The drawing's own last line is the
standing rule: *"Everything here is queued, and nothing is sent."*
